questions.question_text:
A cut in a network crosses edges $SA$ (capacity $18$) and $SB$ (capacity $22$), both directed from the source side to the sink side.
What is the capacity of the cut?

options.why: Took the maximum single edge capacity instead of summing all forward cut edges.
Took the minimum single edge capacity instead of summing all forward cut edges.
Subtracted or miscalculated edge weights instead of adding $18 + 22$.

questions.question_text:
A cut separates source side $\{S, B\}$ from sink side $\{A, T\}$.
It crosses edges $SA$ ($26$, $S\to A$), $AB$ ($9$, $A\to B$), and $BT$ ($21$, $B\to T$).
What is the capacity of the cut?

options.why: Added the backward edge $AB$ ($26 + 9 + 21 = 56$) which flows from sink side to source side.
Subtracted the backward edge $AB$ ($47 - 9 = 38$) instead of treating its contribution as zero.
Counted only the first edge leaving the source instead of all forward-crossing edges.

questions.solution_text:
Edge $AB$ flows from sink side $A$ to source side $B$, contributing $0$.
$\text{Cut capacity} = 26 + 21$
$= 47$

questions.question_text:
A line drawn across a network cuts edges $SA$ and $AB$, but leaves the path $S\to C\to T$ completely untouched.
What is the status of this line?

options.text: Not a valid cut, because path $S\text{–}C\text{–}T$ remains uncut.
A valid cut with capacity equal to $w(SA) + w(AB)$.
options.why: Assumed any line intersecting some edges is a valid cut even if paths remain open.

options.text: The minimum cut of the network.
options.why: Confused an incomplete line with the network's minimum bottleneck cut.

options.text: A valid cut because it intersects the source side.
options.why: Believed touching the source side is sufficient to form a valid separation.

questions.solution_text: A valid cut must completely block all flow from source to sink. Since path $S\text{–}C\text{–}T$ is open, it is not a valid cut.

questions.question_text:
Cut $C$ separates $\{S, U\}$ from $\{V, T\}$.
Why is edge $VU$ ($8\text{ L/s}$) excluded when calculating the capacity of cut $C$?

options.text: It flows from the sink side ($V$) to the source side ($U$).
It is the smallest capacity in the entire network.
options.why: Mistakenly believed edge exclusion is based on capacity magnitude rather than direction.

options.text: It does not connect directly to the source or sink vertex.
options.why: Believed only edges touching $S$ or $T$ can contribute to cut capacity.

options.text: It is already fully saturated with maximum flow.
options.why: Confused edge saturation with directional cut capacity definitions.

questions.solution_text: Edges directed from the sink side to the source side carry backflow and contribute $0$ to cut capacity.

questions.question_text:
Cut $K$ separates $\{S, X\}$ from $\{Y, T\}$.
Crossing edges are $SY = 34$ ($S\to Y$), $YX = 12$ ($Y\to X$), and $XT = 28$ ($X\to T$).
What is the capacity of cut $K$?

options.why: Added the backward edge $YX$ ($34 + 12 + 28 = 74$) instead of excluding it.
Subtracted the backward edge capacity ($62 - 12 = 50$) instead of adding zero.
Counted only the edge directly connected to the source.

questions.solution_text:
Edge $YX$ flows backwards from sink side $Y$ to source side $X$.
$\text{Cut capacity} = 34 + 28$
$= 62$

questions.question_text:
On a pipeline network, Cut 1 has forward edges $44$ and $40$.
Cut 2 has forward edges $36$ and $40$, plus a backward edge of $15$.
What are the capacities of Cut 1 and Cut 2?

options.text: $\text{Cut 1} = 84, \text{Cut 2} = 76$
$\text{Cut 1} = 84, \text{Cut 2} = 91$
options.why: Added the backward edge of $15$ to Cut 2 ($36 + 40 + 15 = 91$).

options.text: $\text{Cut 1} = 84, \text{Cut 2} = 61$
options.why: Subtracted the backward edge of $15$ from Cut 2 ($76 - 15 = 61$).

options.text: $\text{Cut 1} = 44, \text{Cut 2} = 36$
options.why: Recorded only the top edge of each cut instead of summing the cut edges.

questions.question_text:
A cut across five pipes cuts forward pipe $A$ ($42\text{ L/s}$), forward pipe $B$ ($38\text{ L/s}$), and backward pipe $C$ ($15\text{ L/s}$).
What is the total flow capacity of this cut?

options.text: $80\text{ L/s}$
$95\text{ L/s}$
options.why: Added backward pipe $C$ ($42 + 38 + 15 = 95$) instead of excluding backflow.

options.text: $65\text{ L/s}$
options.why: Subtracted backward pipe $C$ ($80 - 15 = 65$) instead of setting its contribution to $0$.

options.text: $42\text{ L/s}$
options.why: Selected only the largest single pipe rather than summing all forward pipes.

questions.question_text:
A dashed line crosses edges $SA$ and $SB$, but path $S\to C\to D\to T$ is completely open.
Which statement is correct?

options.text: The line is not a valid cut because path $S\text{–}C\text{–}D\text{–}T$ remains uncut.
The line is a valid cut with capacity $w(SA) + w(SB)$.
options.why: Failed to check whether all source-to-sink paths are severed by the cut line.

options.text: The line is a valid cut because it cuts at least two edges.
options.why: Assumed cutting any two edges guarantees a valid network cut.

options.text: The line has capacity equal to the minimum flow.
options.why: Assumed an invalid cut has a meaningful numerical capacity.

questions.solution_text: A line that leaves any source-to-sink path uncut is not a valid cut.

questions.question_text:
A cut across three feeder lines into a sink has forward capacities $52$, $48$, and $35$.
What is the capacity of this cut?

options.why: Omitted the third edge ($52 + 48 = 100$) when summing the cut capacity.
Arithmetic error when adding $52 + 48 + 35$.
Averaged the edge weights instead of calculating the sum.
